en: Most web applications you'll be building, no
matter if you're using Bun or not,
will need some form of data persistence,
data storage, for example, a database. And
when building an application with Bun,
that can be particularly easy
because you may just wanna use SQLite. And
guess what? Bun has a built-in SQLite
client. And SQLite, in case you don't know,
is an amazing database solution that's often
enough for many applications.
And you don't need a
or any external service for that. Instead,
it'll just be a file on your system, on your
VPS, wherever you're hosting the website.
And Bun has a built-in client for
interacting with it. It's high performance
and it's easy to use with Bun as you'll see.
And to show you, I'm in a brand new project
which you as always find attached.
And in there I have an index.ts file which
has a couple of dummy routes set up. I'm
building a basic notes app here, not super
exciting but useful for this example. And
it's best to just see it so I can run a dev
script which was added here. And if I then
visit localhost:3000, I can create notes
here like a test note. I then see those
notes also down here. I can view them, I can
edit them,
update the note. Here we go. And I can also
delete it.
Obviously nothing fancy but gets the job
done. Now this is all implemented with a
bunch of routes using Bun's serve feature,
which was covered in a separate lecture,
just like the router, using GET and POST
routes here because of course I also have
form submissions for handling the notes data
submitted by the user.
And I got a bunch of views, a bunch of HTML
files, bunch of HTML templates which have
some basic HTML and CSS code and
placeholders like this in the HTML code, and
then a views.ts file which registers all
these HTML files and then contains the logic
for replacing the double curly brace
placeholders with the actual values that
should be injected in there, the actual note
text, for example. You've seen similar
examples in earlier lectures if you went
through them.
In index.ts, I have those routes registered.
Then I got some utility functions for
returning HTML responses, for redirecting,
for parsing an ID because some of these
routes have dynamic segments where I expect
to get the ID of a note, the ID of the note
that should be deleted or the ID of the note
which I wanna edit or where I wanna submit.
The updated version and therefore I parse
that ID and convert it from a string, which
it is in the URL, to a number because I am
using numeric IDs in my database as you'll
just see in a second.
Other than that, there's really nothing
fancy in the index.ts file. Maybe this part
here is interesting. I got some logic in
there to listen for
events where the server is shut down to
perform a clean shutdown. And here,
important, I am closing my database.
Speaking of the database, that is of course
the interesting part in DBTS
because in there we're using Bun's built-in
SQLite client. And again, in case you don't
know,
SQLite is a SQL database which unlike
PostgreSQL or MySQL does not require a
separate database server that needs to be
running somewhere. Instead, it's just a file
that in this case will be managed by Bun, by
that SQLite client that's built into Bun.
It's this notes.sqlite file that was created
for me here,
and the file name is entirely up to you. You
can set it in your code, and I'll get back
to that.
But this is really just your entire
database. It lives on your system, and that
makes it so easy to use during development,
but it's also perfectly viable for
production. I'm using it in many of my
production apps out there because it's easy
to use. You can just back it up by copying
the file in the end and you don't pay for an
extra database server. But that is of course
up to you. How can you use it with Bun
though? Well, Bun has that SQLite package
here and from there you can import a
database class.
You can then instantiate that to register a
new database and here you enter your file
name and that can be anything you want.
Could also be app.db, whatever you want. The
file extension doesn't matter. The file name
doesn't matter, it's entirely up to you.
You can also use the special:memory:
name, which is a reserved name, to create it
in memory only, which of course means the
data will actually be lost when you shut
down the server, which is typically not what
you want from your database. But for
example, if you need a database for your
unit tests, which you want to erase after
every test run, memory could be a good
option. Here, I'm going for a filename to
have an actual file that's persisted.
This constructor then also takes an optional
configuration object where you could, for
example, set up a read-only database if you
only want to use it as a data source and not
store anything in there. You can set create
to true and you don't need to technically.
If you would set this to false and that file
wouldn't exist yet, then it would actually
fail and it would not create it for you. If
you set it to true or omit it, which is the
default,
so true is the default, I mean, then that
database file notes.sqlite in my case will
be created for you if it doesn't exist yet.
strict=true has something to do with
parameters you pass into your queries, and
I'll get back to that and what strict is all
about.
